HEADLINE: Hoffman warns marketers to pull back from digital cliff
TEXT:
Former agency boss turned advertising contrarian Bob Hoffman believes the public and marketers need to wake up to the significant privacy concerns and ineffectiveness in digital advertising.

Mr Hoffman believes digital advertising is overhyped and is, to the danger of the industry, dominated by the Silicon Valley duopoly of Facebook and Google. ‘‘Take away Google and Facebook and the online advertising industry is not growing. They have essentially become the online advertising industry,’’ Mr Hoffman told The Australian Financial Review.

‘‘I don’t understand why governments aren’t taking a close look at the restraint of trade that is happening as a result of the extraordinary amount of power these two have.

’’ According to research by US venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins Caufield Byers, Google and Facebook account for 85¢ in every new digital advertising dollar spent in the US. It is believed to be similar in markets such as Australia.

‘‘They continue to be nontransparent in their practices, they will not allow full third-party auditing, which has been a standard practice in the agency business for years – clients don’t seem to care,’’ Mr Hoffman said.

‘‘We spent decades developing practices so we can understand the relative media value we’re buying through auditing and now these guys won’t agree to that.’’

Both Facebook and Google have been embroiled by advertising scandals over the past 12 months. Facebook has admitted to multiple errors to metrics it providers marketers which impacts their spending.

Google was found to put many of its clients’ advertising on content such as extremist recruitment videos, anti Semitic and anti-feminist content on its video-sharing platform YouTube.

A number of major Australian brands were found to be unwittingly funding piracy via Google’s display advertising network.

‘‘The thing about the brand safety issues with Facebook and Google, I wrote about that years ago, but as soon as that appeared in newspapers, all of a sudden the advertisers pretended they were shocked, they had no idea ... I don’t buy that,’’ Mr Hoffman said.

Mr Hoffman warned that tracking digital advertising is hurting journalism and is concerning from a privacy standpoint. ‘‘The whole essence of online tracking is to follow people from quality websites like The Australian Financial Review, follow them to Bikinibabe.com, and it’s costing you 1/50 what it cost you on a quality website.

‘‘This is not just hurting journalism, it’s hurting society. We have fake news and crappy websites that people are going to all the time and advertisers are sending them money. It’s diminishing the ability of quality media organisations to exist and sending money to the crappiest places possible.

’’ However, Mr Hoffman said the issue is not too far gone to rescue.

‘‘People don’t understand how their privacy and security is being compromised by all this tracking,’’ he said.

He pointed to legislation in the European Union, which will be enforceable in May next year, called the General Data Protection Regulation, which provides tougher rules for the use and privacy of EU citizens’ data.

‘‘This will affect the ability of advertisers to send their ads to crappy locations instead of reaching people on the websites of quality publishers who are developing an audience. I think this is an important step,’’ Mr Hoffman said.

‘‘This is a serious issue for journalism, for the health of democracy and I think the public, when educated about the problems and the dangers of surveillance marketing, will be in agreement that these are needed things.’’

Mr Hoffman will be in Australia in September to deliver the keynote speech for ReThinkTV, run by broadcasting industry lobbying and marketing group ThinkTV.

HEADLINE: AFL, racing in strong push for a Melbourne sports media centre
TEXT:
Horse racing broadcaster Racing.com’s move into the AFL’s Melbourne headquarters could be the precursor for the building of a digital sports media hub as part of the mooted $300 million revamp of Etihad Stadium.

The hub would involve several sports sharing production, studio and editing facilities housed under the one roof and anchored by the AFL. Horse racing would also be a tenant under the plans, with other major sports already having been approached to share the facilities and create a cluster of digital sports media operations.

The AFL bought Etihad Stadium in a $200 million deal last year and is working on a master plan for the facility and surrounding area, for which it is in the midst of negotiations with the Victorian state government for funding.

Part of the revamp is set to include the league’s adjacent headquarters AFL House in a move that would extend the stadium’s footprint over to the Docklands harbour

Racing.com, the broadcasting joint venture between Seven West Media and Racing Victoria, moved into AFL House this month to a dedicated facility in space next to existing AFL Media team of about 100 full- and part-time journalists, editors and producers.

The AFL and horse racing teams will use existing studio facilities built by the AFL and production suites that will continue to be used by the league to produce content such as in-game footage and highlights shown across its social media accounts and websites.

‘‘Our production and studio facility has seen the AFL media team develop engaging and creative content for millions of fans across the AFL digital network,’’ AFL spokesman Jay Clark said.

‘‘The landscape, especially in digital and content consumption is evolving at a rapid pace, this partnership opens the door to collaborate on future creative and content opportunities – allowing the AFL to continue to grow our digital footprint and engage new audiences.’’

Racing.com has moved 20 of its editorial, production and content team to the AFL from Racing Victoria’s administration headquarters next to the Flemington racecourse, and will use the AFL’s studio to cover afternoon thoroughbred racing meetings after AFL Media staff have used the facilities in the mornings.

‘‘We’ve previously had an on-course only broadcasting model but we will be more studio-based now,’’ Racing.com chief executive Andrew Catterall said. ‘‘So we will link with the broadcast and be able to use more statistics, graphics and analysis in our coverage.

‘‘Longer-term we need a permanent solution given we do 3000 hours of live broadcasts per year on a dedicated [free-to-air] sports channel. That could also lead to close cooperation between other sports and the sharing of knowledge and facilities that could be closer as technology evolves.’’

Racing.com recently signed a deal to show South Australian racing but faces intense competition from Tabcorp’s Sky Racing after failing in its appeal to the Australian Competition Tribunal’s decision on the pending merger between Tabcorp and Tatts to have Sky Racing give up some exclusive racing coverage around the country

HEADLINE: Lone Star joins pack tuning in to Network Ten
TEXT:
Private equity and distressed debt firm Lone Star Funds is understood to be one of at least nine parties running the numbers on Network Ten with indicative bids for the free-to-air broadcaster due at the end of August.

The US-based private equity giant, which manages more than $US70 billion ($87.7 billion) globally, has been looking to grow its exposure in Australia.

Lone Star is believed to be among the nine parties that have signed a nondisclosure agreement and picked up an information memorandum (IM), a document detailing Ten’s business and financials.

Sources stressed signing up for an IM by no means guarantees a bid will be forthcoming for Ten, the home of I’m a Celebrity ... Get Me Out of Here! and Shark Tank, from the Texasheadquartered fund – it is not traditionally an investor in media.

Lone Star has historically invested more in real estate and mortgage debt, but is said to have moved to target more distressed debt assets in the AsiaPacific region. Last year it hired former Fortress Investment Group director Jason Howes to source Australian deals for Lone Star.

The 22-year-old firm tried to buy ASX-listed real estate investment trust Astro Japan earlier this year and oil and gas player AWE last year.

Releasing the IM is the first stage in the two-step auction process. Indicative bids are due in late August after advisors PPB Advisory andMoelis& Co pushed back the date so bidders would have more time to get offers prepared.

Lone Star joins fellow private equity giants Oaktree Capital Management, which helped keep Nine Entertainment out of administration in 2012 via a debtfor-equity swap and earlier this month sold its last remaining shares in the company, and New York-based hedge fund Anchorage Capital Group who are also running the ruler over themetropolitan broadcaster.

Ten was put into voluntary administration in June after billionaire shareholders and guarantors of a $200 million Commonwealth Bank of Australia loan Lachlan Murdoch, Bruce Gordon and James Packer signalled they would not back a new $250million cash facility to keep the network going.

The network was in advanced talks with CBS and 21st Century Fox, of which Mr Murdoch is executive chairman, to dramatically cut the high cost of the output deals Ten had with the pair of US studios.

CBS and Ten had put a draft deal together where the US studio would have taken equity in the Australian free-to-air broadcaster in exchange for cutting the price of its programming deal. As Ten’s largest creditor, the US studio has also put in a claim for $795.5 million – the value of Ten’s future payments to CBS over the next five years under its content deal.

CBS is also one of the parties that have picked up an IM on Ten and could potentially bid for the network.

Mr Gordon and Mr Murdoch have long pined for taking greater control of Ten – the former is the network’s largest shareholder with just under 15 per cent via his investment company Birketu, whileMrMurdoch holds around 7.7 per cent through his investment vehicle Illyria. Foxtel, which is 50-50 owned by Telstra and News Corporation, of which Mr Murdoch is co-chairman, owns another 13.9 per cent of Ten.

The pair have formed a joint venture to take over Ten which hinges on the government successfully changing media ownership regulation when Parliament returns in August 8. The billionaires pre-emptively took their proposed acquisition to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission which is slated to give a ruling, or a statement of issues, on August 24.

HEADLINE: Labor bold and smart on tax
TEXT:
It was instructive that the first Coalition response to Labor's move on income splitting on Sunday was to attack the opposition's preparedness to lift the overall tax burden, rather than the features of the policy.

It is instructive because it suggests the Coalition sees this policy for what it is: a politically pragmatic piece of policy that has been well designed to hit where it is supposed to hit.

That makes it a tough one to challenge, and an easier one to (somehow) emulate in the months to come. Labor has once again gone where the major parties have, in the past, feared to tread. But it has done so with some intelligence in its policy design, not a sledgehammer.

The charge that the policy is one that shows Labor wants to "whack the wealthy" seems to miss the point. Voters see large corporates and high income earners apparently paying tax as a matter of choice rather than obligation, so most would think whacking the wealthy a good idea.

What we mostly see in this policy, however, is a confirmation of how the days when the efficiency of tax design, and the ultimate goal of reducing overall taxation, have taken a back seat to other policy drivers.

Bill Shorten and Chris Bowen have nattily dressed up a tax system clean-up - whether this new initiative or previous ones on negative gearing and capital gains tax - in the clothes of their "inequality" agenda.

Their proposal for stopping those who can afford to do so reaping the benefit of the tax-free threshold, which is designed after all to help low-income earners several times over, is a reasonable one. They have limited the impact of the measure - and the political fallout - by keeping farmers out of the policy. But another benefit of discretionary trusts is the opportunity to arbitrage the difference between the top personal tax rate and the company tax rate. Labor is actually increasing that gap through its other policies.

And this highlights how tax policy - on both sides of politics - has now become a patch-up job, with policies developed on this issue or that issue, rather than a comprehensive plan for our tax system as a whole.

Maybe that is all either side is capable of doing at a time when the personal income tax scales have been rendered almost impossible to significantly adjust because of the clunkiness of the rate scale imposed by reckless rounds of tax cuts in the Howard years, and by the straitened budget circumstances of the present day.

The announcement - along with the push for a referendum vote - puts Labor back ahead of the Coalition as the initiator of policy. These announcements are not ones the government can simply ignore: it will be forced to either agree to them or find some complicated reasons why it can't.

Hopefully, this will not be as excruciating a process as that we witnessed on negative gearing.

HEADLINE: Rising job insecurity myth busted
TEXT:
Labour market evidence does not support prominent union claims that job insecurity is increasing and suggests it may in fact be falling, a new study has found.

University of Melbourne economist Jeff Borland, who previously backed unions in the Fair Work Commission's review of penalty rates, released an analysis of labour force data on Friday that showed more workers were staying in jobs longer and fewer were expecting to leave their job due to a temporary contract.

"A higher rate of job churning and insecurity, workers moving through more jobs in their working careers, would imply that average job tenure is decreasing over time," the study said.

"In fact, job tenure has shifted in the opposite direction, with more workers being in long-duration jobs, and fewer in short-duration jobs."

The proportion of women who had been in jobs for 10 years or more had doubled from 1982 to 2016, growing from 12.4 per cent to 25.3 per cent. Men in jobs for 10 years or more had "remained relatively steady" over the same period and men in jobs for less than 12 months had fallen.

To judge if workers employed long term with labour hire companies might be disguising an increase in job insecurity, Professor Borland looked at the latest data from the influential Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey.

He found the number of people employed through a temporary agency had trended down "fairly consistently" from 2001 to 2015, falling from 3.1 per cent of the workforce to 2.2 per cent.

Professor Borland said it also "appears that workers in Australia understand that job security has not declined".

According to Australian Bureau of Statistics data, those expecting to leave their job in the next 12 months due to downsizing or a temporary contract had fallen from 2 per cent to 1.8 per cent in the past decade and a half. Part-time workers who believed they would not be with their current employer had fallen from 15.5 per cent to 12.5 per cent.

The analysis comes as unions and Labor prepare a push against insecure work and casualisation at the next election, as ACTU secretary Sally McManus calls the issue a "nationwide crisis" and calls for greater political action.

Labor has promised to limit who can be a casual worker, regulate labour hire and crack down on sham contracting where an employee is hired as an independent contractor to avoid job protections and minimum pay.

Opposition Leader Bill Shortensaid on Saturday that more than three million workers were in "part-time, casualised and insecure work, all too often under-represented, all too often under-paid and all too often too afraid to complain".

 Professor Borland's analysis follows a paper by economists Inga Lass and Mark Wooden who used the latest HILDA data to show "non-standard employment", including fixed-term contracts and casual work, has been stable for the past 15 years and was a "transitory experience" for many workers.

HEADLINE: CBA developer 'wrong', says Hartnell
TEXT:
A chairman of the Cairns property developer portrayed as a victim of possible illegal lending practices by Commonwealth Bank of Australia said the company paid too much for land and wasn't mistreated by its financier.

Prominent Sydney lawyer Tony Hartnell disagreed with assertions by Small Business Ombudsman Kate Carnell - which were leaked to 60 Minutes - that the bank drove CEC Group into bankruptcy in 2011.

"In retrospect the judgment to develop a large landbank was wrong," Mr Hartnell said in an interview on Friday. "[Chief executive] Roy Lavis wasn't trying to diddle anyone running CEC. He merely took a business decision that turned out to be wrong."

The comments by the first chairman of the Australian Securities Commission and a co-founder of the Atanaskovic Hartnell law firm undermine a report by the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman that said Commonwealth Bank may have committed unconscionable conduct, which is unlawful.

Ms Carnell's findings, which were meant to be confidential, have been used by bank critics to build public support for tougher regulation of the industry.

Mr Hartnell, who served four years on the CEC board, said the company decided to expand by buying land and building housing around Cairns and towns in northern Queensland.

When land prices were rising, the investments were profitable. When the 2007-08 financial crisis hit, CEC was caught out like many other property developers. Worth at $220 million at one point, it went bankrupt in 2011. Mr Lavis wants $200 million compensation for investors.

"At the time [I was on the board] the biggest issue for CEC was to develop a landbank," the 74-year-old Mr Hartnell said. "It was priced to be very sensible. Along came the GFC and a landbank idea is wealth depleting because the prices are falling. In retrospect the judgment to develop a large landbank was wrong.

"The time prior to the GFC was a time of rapidly expanding bank credit in Australia and in retrospect that was probably too quickly and enabled people like CEC and others to grow investments when they really should have been restrained."

Mr Lavis, the CEC chief executive who is now bankrupt, said property development was one quarter of the company and wasn't big enough to send it broke. At the time he praised Commonwealth Bank for its support, comments he has now retracted.

"We were getting quite good profits out of the rest of the company so I can't see how land on its own would tip us over," he said Friday. "What tipped us over was the bank requiring us to pay back debt so quickly."

The CEC case has caused deep hostility between the Commonwealth Bank, Australia's largest, and Ms Carnell, a former Liberal politician appointed to appease the small business sector.

Her March report criticised the bank for pushing CEC to cut debt by selling assets in early 2008 after increasing CEC's loans in late 2007. The report didn't mention the global financial crisis, which hit at the time, nor consider if CEC borrowed too much.

Government sources have expressed unease that Ms Carnell, who used an interview with 60 Minutes to attack the bank, singled out CEC for what she called a "deep dive" investigation when it wasn't a small business.

One of Ms Carnell's officials said CEC became a small company before it went broke. If BHP failed and turned into a small company the ombudsman would be entitled to investigate it too, she said.

Ms Carnell, who has denied leaking her report to 60 Minutes, was not responsible for the decision to investigate CEC, the official said, which was chosen because it met the criteria set by the government for an investigation into the treatment of bank customers.

Federal MP and former CEC chairman Warren Entsch appeared to play an important role behind the scenes turning CEC into a cause celebre. He convinced the government to direct Ms Carnell to investigate people or companies who said they were bank victims, introduced Ms Carnell to CEC and told 60 Minutes about the company, he said last week.

"I have always been open, upfront and proud of my role in CEC, and this experience has only served to give me a better understanding of the events that surrounded CEC at the time," Mr Entsch said in a letter to this newspaper.

Mr Hartnell said, "Warren Entsch believes fervently that the Commonwealth Bank acted unconscionably. I take that at face value. I can't stand up and say the same thing because I have no basis."

Other CEC insiders agree with Mr Hartnell, who was chairman for 18 months and stepped down in 2010, which placed him on the board during the debt negotiations.

A CEC founding director and a former CEC executive have both said that Mr Lavis was ambitious to grow the company and made bad investments that couldn't be recouped. The Commonwealth Bank says it lost almost $60 million on CEC.

An important figure in the company was Brisbane financial consultant Greg Kern, who was an ally of Mr Lavis on the CEC board, sold consulting services to the company and led negotiations with the bank, according to other former directors.

Mr Kern didn't return five phone calls from The Australian Financial Review.

HEADLINE: Trusts tax riles small business
SUBHEAD: Labor to impose 30pc hit on distributions
TEXT:
Labor's plan to impose a 30 per cent tax on distributions from family trusts will hit 198,000 supposed small businesses but many of these are self-classified by high-earning individuals and not actual active businesses, the opposition says.

The other 120,000 trusts to be hit are "pure income splitters".

Labor released the breakdown of the 318,000 discretionary trusts to be affected to fend off what looms as a full-blown campaign by the federal government that the proposed tax is an attack on small business that will sap economic growth and job creation.

Tax experts were generally supportive of the policy with the chief criticism being the politically motivated exemption for farmers, while a "concerned" small business sector will meet the opposition to seek further clarification of the impact.

Peter Strong, chief executive of the Council of Small Business Australia, said Labor was already promising a 49.5 per cent top marginal tax rate, and threatening to undo company tax cuts for small business and reverse cuts to Sunday penalty rates, a cost that would be reimposed on small business.

The trust clampdown, which the Parliamentary Budget Office estimates will raise $4.1 billion over four years and $17 billion over a decade, is one step in Labor leader Bill Shorten's avowed targeting of inequality. Labor has also set its sights on changes to the Fair Work Act to tackle the insecurity and uncertainty associated with what it says is an explosion since the global financial crisis in casual and other non-permanent forms of work.

Shadow workplace relations minister Brendan O'Connor will give a scene-setting speech on Wednesday about "resetting the balance of power in the workforce".

Yesterday, Mr Shorten announced that if elected Labor will tax distributions from family trusts to adults at a minimum 30 per cent.

"Every year in Australia, there are high-income earners who use discretionary trusts to park their money in a lower tax bracket," he told the NSW Labor conference.

"Our system should not be subsidising those who are already wealthy - and our budget cannot afford to."

As forecast, the policy will not abolish the use of trusts for asset protection or succession planning and it will not apply to farmers, charities, deceased estates, disability fixed or unit trusts.

The tax change will affect 2 per cent of taxpayers and 318,000 trusts, about half the 642,000 discretionary trusts in Australia. Shadow treasurer Chris Bowen said the practice of wealthy people setting up trusts solely to distribute income to elderly parents, non-working children and spouses to avoid paying the top marginal tax rate was legal but "can't be allowed to continue". Farmers were exempted because they often have "lumpy income".

Treasurer Scott Morrison called on Labor to release the costings and detail of the policy. He said combined with the possibility Labor may reverse the legislated company tax cuts for businesses with annual turnovers capped at $50 million, the trust tax would be a double-whammy for small business.

"This is another direct assault on small businesses by Labor. Bill Shorten is whacking small business families with a double tax."

Mr Shorten told the government to "get out and smell the roses".

"Seriously, what is the case for income splitting in discretionary trusts for these fortunate few?"

Mr Bowen said there were "many, many hundreds of thousands who are small businesses in Australia and most don't use discretionary trusts".

Robert Deutsch, senior tax counsel for the Tax Institute, said it was a "clever and surgical" approach to address "what people think is the main problem with discretionary trusts" because it avoided the complexity and unintended consequences of trying to tax them as companies. His main concern was that it exempted farmers, who are significant users of such trusts.

"There is no genuine policy basis for the farm carve-out," he said.

Tony Greco, general manager of technical policy for the Institute of Public Accountants, concurred.

"Labor is pitting small business owners against farmers," he said.

He said lumpy income was no grounds for an exemption, especially as farmers already have access to the farm income deposit scheme which enables them to park income in good years and draw it down in bad years, when it is then assessed for income tax.

Mr Greco suggested small businesses could circumvent the change by abolishing the trust and making a non-working spouse a partner.

Mark Molesworth, a tax partner with BDO, said relatively low-income families could be caught unintentionally.

"A husband and wife, each of whom is a nurse earning $70,000 per year, will pay, in aggregate, $31,400 in tax on total family income of $140,000," he said.

"A husband and wife, each of whom is a plumber, carry on business through a discretionary trust and earn a net profit of $140,000. They will pay, in aggregate, $42,000 under Labor's plan."

HEADLINE: Buffett's solar farm basks in sweet spot
TEXT:
Topaz Solar Farm manager Gary Hood doesn't have solar panels on the roof of his home in San Luis Obispo County because he doesn't need them.

Directly outside his two-level homestead, nestled into the foothills of the Carrizo Plain, are the 8.4 million solar panels that make up BHE Renewables' Topaz Solar Farm. With a capacity of 550 megawatts it is one of the largest solar farms in California.

The $3 billion Topaz Solar Farm was the largest utility-scale solar project in the world when completed in 2014.

Now it has to settle for being the second-largest solar farm in California, which has embraced renewable energy as part of its push to have 50 per cent clean energy by 2030.

There are more than 23,500 gigawatt hours in operation across the state, which, like Australia, is blessed with abundant sunshine.

The state's largest solar project is the 579 megawatt Solar Star project, near Rosamond. Also owned by BHE, it was completed this year. The Desert Sunlight project in the Mojave Desert, in the state's south-east, is the same size as Topaz, while there are also four other 200-megawatt to 250-megawatt projects in California.

The Topaz solar farm was developed by company First Solar before being bought by Berkshire Hathaway Renewables, a subsidiary of the multinational company run by billionaire Warren Buffett, which has more than 1400 megawatts of solar projects in the US.

Sceptical local communities worried about the impact of the Topaz Solar Farm on local wildlife and flora were reassured by the San Luis Obispo County's rigorous development and environmental approvals processes.

"I think a lot of people didn't think it could be done and some environmental groups were against building a large-scale project in this area," Mr Hood told The Australian Financial Review between rows of solar panels at the Topaz facility.

"But First Solar and Berkshire Hathaway, we showed the world it could be done. There were a lot of big solar projects being built at the same time, but we had a lot more restrictions on it. There were 133 environmental conditions on what we could do."

The Topaz solar plant consists of 22 sections or "blocks" of thin-film cadmium telluride PV panels across 4700 acres. It produces enough electricity to power 18,000 Californian homes and displaces about 377,000 tonnes of carbon, equivalent to taking 73,000 cars off the road. The barbed-wire steel fences have a double bar at the bottom to allow the endangered kit fox to slip through. Antelopes and elks also live between the solar sections, while sheep graze between the panels to keep the grass under control.

San Luis Obispo County is a renewable energy "sweet spot" with 308 days of sunshine every year. Unlike most solar and wind projects in regional Australia, which need to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to connect to the grid, the Topaz site, a former ranch, was chosen because it was right next to a transmission line that connects to Bakersfield, the substation hub for the electricity grid between the north and south of California. It is also linked to the coast via the nearest big town of San Luis Obispo and then connects to Los Angeles. Under an advantageous power purchase agreement with the state's largest energy utility Pacific Gas & Electric, Topaz Solar Farm has locked in a deal that delivers about US60¢ a kilowatt hour for the power it puts into the grid.

With the advent of more solar projects, the price offered for solar power has come down to about US30¢ a kilowatt hour, or about half of what Topaz receives. (The flipside is that the cost of building new solar farms has fallen dramatically in recent years due to new and cheaper technology.)

While the Topaz farm employed about 1000 people during construction, it only needs 15 staff now to monitor and replace broken panels. Low operational costs are an upside compared with traditional fuel sources.

Mr Hood, who has helped BHE deliver projects across the US including 1 megawatt community solar units, said he was not fussed about the emergence of larger solar projects. "We would love to expand because the solar resources here are perfect," he said. "But the way it works it was so hard to permit this with the county, it would be a nightmare to go back and try and build more."

 Under an agreement with environmental groups, the site will be handed back to the Department of Fish and Wildlife after 35 years.

The reporter travelled to California with the assistance of the Climate Council.

HEADLINE: MBA scholarship worth $60,000 up for grabs
TEXT:
Applications are open for the prestigious 2018 BOSS Emerging Leader Scholarship which will award the winner with a free MBA degree from the University of Sydney Business School.

People have until September 18 to lodge applications and, if short-listed, they will advance through a further three selection rounds until the winner is announced on November 10.

In addition to the free MBA degree worth $60,000, the winner will also have the opportunity for media training with The Australian Financial Review and to publish an opinion piece in BOSS magazine.

Recent winners say the experience of doing the MBA at the University of Sydney Business School has been both challenging and worthwhile.

"In each of the subjects there are a number of things I've applied. It's changed the way I deal with my fellow employees and the way I give feedback to people that report to me," said Samantha Cook, the 2016 scholarship winner.

Ms Cook, who is a senior associate at the Pacific Legal Network, is more than halfway through the MBA. It's been a challenge fitting in the demands of university with a full-time job but she said it had been worth it.

"It's knowing you can't commit to everything in life and knowing that sometimes things have to give. Sometimes that means a bit on your social life," she said.

Peter Giurissevich, the BOSS MBA scholarship winner for 2017, is also learning to juggle his commitments.

"It's really a time management thing more than anything else. You have your day at work then you go home and put the kids to bed and then find some time to do reading and catch up on any uni work," he said.

Mr Giurissevich, who is senior counsel for the National Rugby League, has the C-suite in his sights.

"I'm doing the MBA to move into a more commercial role," he said.

"I want to end up a chief executive or a chief operating officer. I can see myself getting a CEO role at one of the NRL clubs or the A-League clubs; cut my teeth as a CEO at that level and then one day having a CEO role with one of the governing bodies: AFL, NRL, soccer or rugby union."

Cook is more circumspect about what she'll do when she completes the course. "I'm keeping an open mind and seeing what opportunities present themselves," she said. "But having done this it's widened my view of the world and I think I might want to do something entirely different."

To apply for the BOSS Emerging Leaders MBA Scholarship 2018, visit bossemergingleaders.com.au.

HEADLINE: Labor members push to accept Palestinian state
TEXT:
The Labor Party, which played a significant role in the formation of Israel in 1948, is moving towards early recognition of a separate Palestinian state.

Motions passed at ALP state and territory conferences over the weekend urge a future Labor government to recognise the state of Palestine.

State ALP conference resolutions are not binding on any future federal Labor government but the pressure will increase on Labor leader Bill Shorten if a similar motion is passed at the party's national conference, scheduled for July next year.

After the NSW motion was carried, former Labor premier Bob Carr described it as "an historic shift in Labor sentiment. It means the party is prepared to back its support for a two-state solution by recognising Palestine just as it recognises Israel. If there's one fact that explains this shift, it's the constant spread of Israeli settlements on occupied Palestinian land."

Currently, federal Labor endorses a two-state solution, consisting of Israel and a separate state of Palestine, and it has previously shied away from immediate recognition of a Palestinian state.

The significance of a NSW Labor conference vote taken late yesterday is that it is backed by a coalition of NSW right and left-wing MPs.

This same coalition would be likely to constitute a majority in any federal ALP caucus - the ultimate decision-making body in a Labor government.

The final resolution carried at the NSW conference was a watered-down version of the one on the notice paper, reflecting new wording introduced at a NSW ALP right-wing faction meeting on Friday night.

 The watering down followed what ALP insiders say was an intense lobbying campaign from officials in the Israeli Embassy in Canberra. Pushing back was pressure from NSW ALP branches, especially in Sydney's western suburbs, where there is a significant Arab Muslim community.

Mr Carr, who once headed a "friends of Israel" group, has since become a passionate critic of Israeli settlements inside the occupied territories. After Friday night's meeting of the right faction in the NSW ALP, which Mr Carr attended, he tweeted: "Recognition of Palestine historic. No ifs or buts. No conditions."

 Resolutions carried by the Queensland and ACT ALP conferences also called for a future ALP government to move towards the "immediate" recognition of a Palestinian state, although the Queensland motion supported "the right of Israel and Palestine to exist within secure internationally recognised borders".

 As inaugural president of the UN, then Australian external affairs minister, Dr H.V. Evatt, played a significant role in the UN vote to back the formation of Israel. However, following the 1967 six-day war the Whitlam government supported UN General Assembly resolutions which called on Israel to withdraw from the Occupied Territories.
